nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Victorian period, Pre-Raphaelite circle
literary_identity: Poet; the finest English devotional lyric poet of the century and a central figure of the Pre-Raphaelite circle.
biography: Born in London on 5 December 1830, youngest child of Gabriele Rossetti, an Italian political exile and Dante scholar, and Frances Polidori; sister of Dante Gabriel and William Michael Rossetti. Devoutly Anglo-Catholic from adolescence, she broke two engagements on religious grounds, and lived a retired life of writing, devotional work and, from 1876, teaching at the St Mary Magdalene penitentiary at Highgate. Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862) was illustrated by her brother; The Prince's Progress (1866), Sing-Song (1872) and A Pageant and Other Poems (1881) followed, and she wrote the carol 'In the Bleak Midwinter' for Scribner's Monthly in 1872. She died of cancer in London on 29 December 1894.
literary_profile: Rossetti's poetry is small in compass and absolute in control: short lyric forms, plain diction, a strict metrical discipline and an imagery that is simultaneously devotional, erotic and deathly. Goblin Market is her one long poem, a fairy-tale narrative of temptation and redemption that has been read as an allegory of the Eucharist, of sisterhood, of sexual knowledge and of the Victorian market. Her later work turns increasingly to the preparation for death, and the sonnets 'Remember' and 'A Birthday' are among the most anthologised poems in English.
stylistic_characteristics: Simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme; refrain and repetition used as a devotional instrument; sensuous and often grotesque imagery of fruit, hair, jewels and flowers; a quiet, unemphatic voice; the deliberate bareness of the late devotional poems.
intellectual_concerns: Temptation, sacrifice and redemption; the sisterhood of women; the body and its dangers; death, the grave and the afterlife; the relation of earthly to divine love; the position of women within the Anglo-Catholic church.
historical_significance: Christina Rossetti is the central woman poet of Victorian England and the finest religious lyricist after Herbert. Goblin Market is a founding text for the modern criticism of Victorian sexuality and of women's writing, and her influence runs through the twentieth-century devotional lyric and through the feminist recovery of the 1970s and 1980s.

W. M. Rossetti); The Face of the Deep (devotional prose, 1892); Called to Be Saints (devotional prose, 1881); Letter and Spirit (devotional prose, 1883); Time Flies: A Reading Diary (1885); Seek and Find (1879); Maude (juvenile prose, written 1850, published 1897).

literary_identity: Poet, painter and translator; the founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood and the central figure of the aesthetic poetry of the 1860s-70s.
biography: Born in London on 12 May 1828, son of Gabriele Rossetti; trained at Sass's academy and the Royal Academy Schools, and in 1848 founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood with Holman Hunt and Millais. He painted The Girlhood of Mary Virgin (1849) and Ecce Ancilla Domini (1850), wrote the Germ (1850), and after the death of his wife Elizabeth Siddal in 1862 buried his poems in her coffin, then exhumed them in 1869 to publish Poems (1870). The 1871 attack by Robert Buchanan ('The Fleshly School of Poetry') began a scandal that damaged his reputation; his health and eyesight failed, and he died at Birchington-on-Sea on 9 April 1882.
literary_profile: Rossetti's poetry is the literary counterpart of his painting: a sensuous, heavily jewelled and incantatory verse of visionary women, of the moment between life and death, and of a synaesthetic correspondence of sound, colour and scent. He translated the early Italian poets (Dante's Vita Nuova, the stilnovisti) and the ballad tradition, and he made the sonnet sequence The House of Life a record of love as both spiritual and physical. His late poems are simpler and more elegiac.
stylistic_characteristics: Rich, slow, alliterative lines with a high proportion of vowel sound; archaic and medievalising diction; the sonnet sequence; the ballad with supernatural machinery; pictorial description that catalogues jewels, hair and flowers; a pervasive atmosphere of dream and suspended time.
intellectual_concerns: Love as a religion, sacred and erotic; the dead beloved and the cult of Beatrice; the relation of the poet to the painter; time, mortality and the permanence of art; the body and the soul; Italy and the medieval past as an alternative to Victorian industrial England.
historical_significance: Rossetti founded Pre-Raphaelitism and gave the aesthetic movement its central images and its doctrine of art for beauty's sake; The House of Life is the major English sonnet sequence of the century after Barrett Browning, and the Buchanan controversy is the decisive episode in the Victorian debate over the morality of art. His influence on Swinburne, Morris, Pater, Wilde and Yeats is direct.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: The Early Italian Poets (translations, 1861; reissued as Dante and His Circle, 1874); Poems (1870); The House of Life (sonnet sequence, in Poems 1870 and Ballads and Sonnets 1881); Ballads and Sonnets (1881); Hand and Soul (prose tale, in the Germ, 1850); Sonnets for Pictures (in the Germ, 1850); Jenny (written 1848-70, published 1870); The Blessed Damozel (written 1847; published in the Germ 1850; revised 1856, 1870); Dante's Inferno (unfinished translation); Collected Works (posthumous, 2 vols, 1886, ed. nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the lyric, the verse essay and the poetry of immigration
literary_identity: Poet and essayist; the author of 'The New Colossus', the sonnet inscribed on the Statue of Liberty, and the first American poet of the Jewish immigrant.
biography: Born Emma Lazarus in New York on 22 July 1849 into a wealthy Sephardi Jewish family; she published her first book at seventeen and was encouraged by Emerson. In the 1880s the Russian pogroms turned her into a Zionist and a campaigner for the Jewish refugees, producing Songs of a Semite (1882) and The Dance to Death (1882), and 'The New Colossus' (1883) for the Bartholdi Pedestal Fund. She died in New York on 19 November 1887, aged thirty-eight.
literary_profile: Lazarus wrote the American poetry of immigration: 'The New Colossus' is the most quoted American sonnet and the founding poem of American immigration, and Songs of a Semite is the first English book of poetry to treat the Jewish people as a nation with a modern destiny. She was also a considerable critic and essayist, and her work marks the moment when American poetry began to speak for the immigrant and the exile.
stylistic_characteristics: The classical sonnet and the verse drama in a formal, measured style; the prophetic and biblical idiom; the rhetoric of the verse address; the essay of cultural argument; the elegy for a persecuted people; the image that becomes a national symbol.
intellectual_concerns: Immigration, exile and the promised land; the Jewish people and the Zionist idea; slavery, persecution and emancipation; American national identity; the city and the harbour; women's education and the woman writer.
historical_significance: Emma Lazarus is the first American poet of immigration and the author of the most famous American sonnet: 'The New Colossus' is inscribed on the Statue of Liberty and has been read by millions, Songs of a Semite founded the literature of American Zionism, and her work made the immigrant experience a central subject of American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Poems and Translations (1866); Admetus and Other Poems (1871); Alide: An Episode of Goethe's Life (1874); The Spagnoletto (1876); Poems and Ballads of Heine (translation, 1881); Songs of a Semite: The Dance to Death and Other Poems (1882); The Feet of the Prophet (1883); 'The New Colossus' (1883, inscribed on the Statue of Liberty 1903); By the Waters of Babylon (1887); The Poems of Emma Lazarus (2 vols, 1889, posthumous); An Epistle to the Hebrews (1882-83, essays).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Southern lyric, the poetry of music and the critical essay
literary_identity: Poet, musician and critic; the finest Southern poet of the postwar generation and the founder of the scientific criticism of English verse.
biography: Born Sidney Clopton Lanier in Macon, Georgia, on 3 February 1842; he served in the Confederate army, was captured and imprisoned at Point Lookout, where he contracted tuberculosis, and after the war taught, played the flute professionally and wrote poetry. He published Poems (1877), The Science of English Verse (1880) and The English Novel (1883), and died at Lynn, North Carolina, on 7 September 1881, aged thirty-nine.
literary_profile: Lanier wrote the Southern lyric after the war: his poems of the Georgia marshes, the Chattahoochee and the sea are the finest American poetry of nature written between Whitman and Frost, and his theory of verse as a form of music — The Science of English Verse — is the founding work of American prosody. He is the central literary figure of the post-war South, and his 'Marshes of Glynn' is one of the great American poems.
stylistic_characteristics: Long, musical, rhythmically inventive lines; the cataloguing of natural detail; the orchestral repetition and the symphonic structure; the fusion of music and metre; the Southern landscape and the memory of the war.
intellectual_concerns: Nature, the marsh and the sea; music and the theory of verse; the South after the war and the memory of the Confederacy; mortality and the shortness of life; the trade of poetry and the struggle for a living; God and the natural world.
historical_significance: Lanier is the finest Southern poet of his generation and the founder of the scientific study of English versification: 'The Marshes of Glynn' and 'The Symphony' are permanent American poems, The Science of English Verse changed the study of prosody, and his example made the post-war South a place where poetry could be written again.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Tiger-Lilies (1867); Poems (Lanier, 1877); The Science of English Verse (1880); 'The Marshes of Glynn' (1878); 'The Symphony' (1875); 'The Song of the Chattahoochee' (1877); The Boy's Froissart (1878); The English Novel (1883, posthumous); Poems of Sidney Lanier (1884, posthumous); Letters of Sidney Lanier (1899, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the dialect poem, the Hoosier sketch and the poetry of childhood
literary_identity: Poet; the 'Hoosier Poet', the most popular American verse writer of the 1890s and the master of the American dialect poem.
biography: Born James Whitcomb Riley in Greenfield, Indiana, on 7 October 1849; he left school early, worked as a sign painter, a travelling salesman and a newspaperman, and made his name with the dialect poems of The Old Swimmin'-Hole and 'Leven More Poems (1883). He toured as a reciter, published over thirty books, and was honoured by the state of Indiana with a memorial day on his birthday. He died in Indianapolis on 22 July 1916.
literary_profile: Riley wrote the American poetry of small-town childhood and of the rural Midwest: his Hoosier dialect poems — 'Little Orphant Annie', 'The Old Swimmin'-Hole', 'When the Frost Is on the Punkin' — were recited in every American school and home, and they made him the most popular poet in the country. He is the central figure of the American dialect school, and his work preserves the speech and the humour of the Indiana of his boyhood.
stylistic_characteristics: Dialect verse with exact phonetic spelling; the child's monologue; the sentimental recollection of the rural past; strong rhythm and easy rhyme for recitation; comic narrative and tall tale in verse; the homely image and the moral ending.
intellectual_concerns: Childhood and the memory of the rural home; the small town and its characters; the passing of the old farm life; the family and the fireside; death and the consolation of memory; the American Midwest.
historical_significance: Riley is the most popular American poet of the 1890s and the central figure of the American dialect school: 'Little Orphant Annie' became a permanent American children's poem, his recitations filled theatres across the country, and he is the essential literary record of the small-town American Midwest before the machine.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: The Old Swimmin'-Hole and 'Leven More Poems (1883); The Boss Girl (1886); Afterwhiles (1888); Pipes o' Pan at Zekesbury (1889); Rhymes of Childhood (1890); Neighborly Poems (1891); Old Fashioned Roses (1889); Green Fields and Running Brooks (1892); Poems Here at Home (1893); Armazindy (1894); A Child-World (1896); Home-Folks (1900); The Book of Joyous Children (1902); His Pa's Romance (1903); Songs o' Cheer (1905); The Complete Works of James Whitcomb Riley (10 vols, 1913).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the dramatic lyric, the New England character poem and the modern narrative
literary_identity: Poet; the founder of modern American poetry in traditional forms, and the first American poet to make a whole town the subject of his art.
biography: Born Edwin Arlington Robinson at Head Tide, Maine, on 22 December 1869 and raised in Gardiner, Maine; he studied at Harvard for two years, worked in New York in poverty, and published The Torrent and the Night Before (1896) and The Children of the Night (1897) at his own expense. Theodore Roosevelt gave him a government post in 1905; he won the Pulitzer Prize three times (1922, 1925, 1928) and died in New York on 6 April 1935.
literary_profile: Robinson wrote the modern American poetry of character: his Tilbury Town poems — portraits of failures, misers, drunkards and quiet desperate lives — are the first great American poems of the small town seen without sentiment, and his long narratives of Arthurian and modern life made him the finest American narrative poet of his age. He kept the traditional forms while the modernists broke them, and his plain, ironic style made him the bridge between Victorian and modern American poetry.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, colloquial line in traditional metre; the dramatic monologue and the character sketch; irony held under tight formal control; the sonnet and the quatrain; the long narrative in blank verse; the ending that withholds consolation.
intellectual_concerns: Failure, loneliness and quiet desperation; the small New England town and its outcasts; marriage and the unlived life; money, drink and decline; the Arthurian legend and the modern quest; the American individual and his illusions.
historical_significance: Robinson is the first major modern American poet and the founder of the American poetry of the small town: his Tilbury Town poems changed American poetry, he won the Pulitzer Prize three times, and his example made it possible for American poets to be both traditional and modern — the bridge from Dickinson and Hardy to Frost and the moderns.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: The Torrent and the Night Before (1896); The Children of the Night (1897); Captain Craig (1902); The Town down the River (1910); The Man against the Sky (1916); Merlin (1917); Lancelot (1920); The Three Taverns (1920); Avon's Harvest (1921); Collected Poems (1921); Roman Bartholow (1923); The Man Who Died Twice (1924); Dionysus in Doubt (1925); Tristram (1927); Sonnets, 1889-1927 (1928); Cavender's House (1929); The Glory of the Nightingales (1930); Matthias at the Door (1931); Nicodemus (1932); Talifer (1933); Amaranth (1934); King Jasper (1935).

birthplace: Near Redwood Falls, Minnesota, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Santee Dakota; the Native American autobiography and the literature of the assimilation debate
literary_identity: Physician, writer and activist; the first Native American to qualify in medicine in the United States and the most widely read Native American author of his generation.
biography: Born Hakadah, later named Ohiyesa, near Redwood Falls, Minnesota, on 19 February 1858, of a Santee Dakota family that fled to Canada after the 1862 uprising; he was raised in the traditional way until his father sent for him at fifteen, and he then took the name Charles Alexander Eastman and studied at Dartmouth and Boston University, graduating in medicine in 1890. He was the physician at Pine Ridge during the Wounded Knee massacre, became a national spokesman for Native rights, and wrote eleven books. He died in Detroit on 8 January 1939.
literary_profile: Eastman wrote the Native American autobiography at its most readable: Indian Boyhood is the classic account of a traditional Dakota childhood, and its companion volumes — The Soul of the Indian, From the Deep Woods to Civilization — record the passage from one world to another with a dignity and a clarity that made them the most widely read Native American books of the period. He was also a central figure in the debate over assimilation, and his work presents the Native case to a white readership without bitterness.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, unhurried expository prose; the remembered detail of the traditional life; the comparative explanation of Dakota belief for a white audience; the narrative of the journey from the woods to the university; the appeal to a common humanity.
intellectual_concerns: Dakota childhood, hunting and the traditional education; the passage from the traditional world to white civilisation; the massacre at Wounded Knee and the betrayal of the treaties; Native religion and its relation to Christianity; the education of the Indian and the policy of assimilation.
historical_significance: Eastman is the most widely read Native American author of his generation and the central figure of the assimilation debate: Indian Boyhood is the classic Native American autobiography, The Soul of the Indian is the foundational account of Dakota religion in English, and his work made the Native American case known to a mass white readership.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Indian Boyhood (1902); Red Hunters and the Animal People (1904); Old Indian Days (1907); Wigwam Evenings (with Elaine Goodale Eastman, 1909); The Soul of the Indian (1911); Indian Child Life (1913); Indian Scout Talks (1914); The Indian Today (1915); From the Deep Woods to Civilization (1916); Indian Heroes and Great Chieftains (1918).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; Victorian prose, historiography and social criticism
literary_identity: Essayist, historian, translator and social prophet; the great Victorian prose stylist and the moralist against whom the age measured itself.
biography: Born on 4 December 1795, son of a stonemason and Calvinist farmer; educated at Annan Academy and Edinburgh University, where he trained for the ministry and abandoned it. He translated Goethe's Wilhelm Meister (1824) and wrote the Life of Schiller (1825) before his marriage in 1826 to Jane Baillie Welsh, whose letters became one of the great documents of the age. Sartor Resartus appeared in Fraser's Magazine in 1833-34, The French Revolution in 1837, Chartism in 1840, On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History in 1841, Past and Present in 1843, Oliver Cromwell's Letters and Speeches in 1845 and the History of Friedrich II of Prussia in six volumes (1858-65). He gave the lectures that made him famous in 1837-40, refused all honours including the offer of the laureateship, and after Jane's death in 1866 wrote little; he died in Chelsea on 5 February 1881.
literary_profile: Carlyle invented the Victorian prose of prophecy: a style built on capitalised abstractions, apostrophe, Hebraic parallelism, exclamation and a ferocious irony, which he used to indict utilitarianism, laissez-faire political economy, parliamentary talk and the 'cash nexus'. His method in history is to make a document speak — the French Revolution as a 'terrible purification', Cromwell's letters as the voice of a man of God — and his theory of the hero, stated in 1841, was the most influential Victorian account of history as the work of great men. He turned German idealism and Goethe's aesthetics into the common currency of English thought.
stylistic_characteristics: Incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences; invented compounds and archaisms; abrupt transitions between the prophetic, the comic and the documentary; direct address to the reader and a self-dramatising narrator; the quotation of primary documents in extenso; the use of symbols (the clothes philosophy, the 'everlasting Yea').
intellectual_concerns: The spiritual condition of the age and the loss of faith; work, the gospel of labour and the dignity of the manual worker; hero-worship and the great man in history; the French Revolution as judgment; the 'cash nexus' and the failure of political economy; silence, sincerity and the contempt of talk; the state and the aristocracy of talent.
historical_significance: Carlyle was the most influential prose writer in Victorian Britain: his French Revolution changed the writing of history, On Heroes supplied the century's theory of leadership, Past and Present its critique of industrialism, and Sartor Resartus its spiritual autobiography. He shaped Ruskin, Arnold, Dickens (to whom he lent the French Revolution while Hard Times was being written), Froude, Kingsley, George Eliot's early criticism and the American Transcendentalists; the twentieth-century reaction against his authoritarianism has not diminished his formal influence on English prose.
